testimony.witness_title: Superintendent, Pawnee Indian Agency, Pawnee, Oklahoma
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on releasing Indians from Government supervision
testimony.subject: Effect of granting fee patents to Indians in the Pawnee Agency area; status of Pawnee, Ponca, Otoe, Kaw, and Tonkawa tribal allotments
testimony.key_claims: Sound judgment has not always been exercised in granting fee patents; many recipients have not used the privilege wisely; young, old, and uneducated Indians should be protected as long as possible. Original allotments: Pawnee 820-830 allotments covering 112,701-113,701 acres; Ponca 782-783 allotments covering 100,745 acres; Otoe 514 allotments covering 128,251-138,351 acres; Kaw 347 allotments covering 99,644 acres; Tonkawa 73 allotments covering 11,466 acres. Approximately three-fifths of the whole area is now restricted. The tendency to share resources with relatives discourages individual financial advancement. All Indians under this jurisdiction are citizens of Oklahoma. Indian laziness is better described as disinclination; reliance on restricted relatives who receive oil and rental income allows patented Indians to avoid work. References personal service history at Sioux, Kiowa, Arapaho, Eastern Cherokee, Puyallup, Oneida, and Pawnee jurisdictions.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Ponca Sub-agency, Pawnee Agency, Oklahoma
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on releasing Indians from Government supervision
testimony.subject: Record of patent-in-fee Indians on the Ponca Reservation
testimony.key_claims: Record of patent-in-fee Indians on Ponca Reservation is not good. Most recipients either sell the patented land or mortgage it immediately after getting the patent. They then spend money on high-powered automobiles and other non-essentials. Restricted Indians are making a living from their lands generally by leasing for agricultural, oil and gas mining purposes. Named individuals: Albert Primeaux sold land for about $600; Maggie LaDue sold all but 80 acres for $3000, land mortgaged; Amarbe LaDue (Otoe) blew in all land and money, now gone to work; George Primeaux deeded land to children keeping life use, doing well; Mike Roy patented, good farmer with oil income; George Smith all patented all sold; Frank Eagle all patented all sold; Dick Gayton all patented and sold, broke, booze fighter; Ben Told wife has 120 acres in trust worth $12,000, Ben loves automobiles and does not like work; George Smith Jr. holds land mortgaged for $6000-$6500 leased for five years. These Indians can be reached at Whiteagle, Oklahoma. Older restricted Indians and minor Indians with land held in trust are fairly prosperous.

testimony.witness_title: Clerk in Charge, Kaw Sub-agency, 34 years in Service
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on releasing Indians from Government supervision
testimony.subject: Kaw Indians who received certificates of competency and disposition of their property
testimony.key_claims: About three-fourths of young adult Indians who received patents were harmed rather than helped. Old Indians and minors who still hold land in trust are fairly prosperous. For Kaw Indians, a certificate of competency removes restrictions from the entire homestead. A list was made of all Kaw Indians who received restricted deeds and have since been given certificates of competency. Detailed property status for approximately 60 named Kaw Indians provided. Great care should be exercised in removing restrictions. Many Kaw Indians are perfectly competent but have not asked for certificates because Kaw Treaty requires written applications. The incompetent is usually the one who makes the most effort to get restrictions removed. Certificates should be granted only after careful examination. Homestead of old Indians should be protected. Ablebodied, educated, trained men with business ability should be given certificates. Capable educated young men who refuse to work should be turned loose so necessity disciplines them.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Tonkawa Sub-agency, Pawnee Agency, Oklahoma
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on releasing Indians from Government supervision
testimony.subject: Experience with fee patent Indians over eleven years at Tonkawa Sub-agency
testimony.key_claims: In eleven years in service, only one Indian (Lona Ciserneos, Tonkawa, Tonkawa Oklahoma) is accumulating property after receiving fee patent; credit given to her hard-working economical Mexican husband. Robert Tah, Railroad Cisco, and David Williams, all Tonkawas at Apache Oklahoma, received fee patents to all lands within last three years and immediately converted them to money spent on expensive automobiles, Indian toggery, gambling. They are now living from money wheedled from relatives. Old dependent Indians receiving $100 monthly are barely able to exist as funds are divided among many relatives. Indians prefer $10,000 in hand over promise of $100 next week. If it were up to reporter, would turn all able-bodied educated Indians loose reserving 20 acres for home completed from their individual funds; uneducated and old dependent Indians would be placed in community system. Indian will not work for himself as long as he has resources; after property is gone they will work. Generally Indians are not satisfied; believe Government employees are in league with grafters. Condition of fee patent Indians is not as good as when under Government jurisdiction.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Otoe Sub-agency, Red Rock Oklahoma
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on condition of fee patent Indians
testimony.subject: Condition of fee patent Indians at Otoe Sub-agency
testimony.key_claims: Fee patent Indians are not as well off as when under Government control. Those who sold land spent money on expensive automobiles, Indian toggery, and gambling. Old dependent Indians receiving $100/month are scarcely able to exist because funds are divided among so many. Indians prefer $10,000 in hand to promise of $100 next week. Recommends turning loose able-bodied and well-educated Indians while establishing a community system for uneducated and old dependent ones. Would reserve 20 acres for a home from individual funds before turning over property.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Pawnee Agency, Pawnee Oklahoma
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on condition of fee patent Indians
testimony.subject: Condition of fee patent Indians at Pawnee Agency
testimony.key_claims: Going too fast in releasing Indians from Government supervision. Named individuals doing well: Louis Matlock, Eva N. Cummings. Named individuals in this class and some in bad shape: George Haymond, Jobie Taylor, Wilber Eaves, Gorden Shaw, Henry Chapman, Willie Lewis, Robert Peters, James Little Sun, Joe Taylor, Elmer Echo Hawk. Recommends giving fee patent but reserving 40 acres; if individual found capable after investigation, might be given full fee patent. Majority very anxious to get liberty then sorry of outcome.

testimony.witness_title: Agent Farmer, Pawnee Agency, Pawnee Oklahoma
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on condition of fee patent Indians
testimony.subject: Condition of fee patent Indians at Pawnee Agency
testimony.key_claims: Indians that received fee patents sold their land and spent all money and are in debt. Not one out of ten who have not sold their land. Some satisfied with how they spent money; others see they made a mistake. Recommends issuing fee patent for part of allotment and holding at least 40 acres in trust. Very few who received fee patent to allotments still own them today. Department gave out about 81 patents; not more than 10 still have their land.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Shawnee Agency area

testimony.key_claims: Acknowledges receipt of circular letter March 24 1921. Those who gained from fee patents: Emmit Pearson (Ralston OK), George Gover (Pawnee OK), Frank Rouwalk (Pawnee OK). Those who have not gained: Clarence Field, Wallace Murie, Caroline Murie, Maggie Knife Chief, Thomas Hand, John Howell, Maude Hand (all Pawnee OK). Most have disposed of allotments and must labor. Not easy for Indian to secure position because whites claim Indians won't work. Most have heired lands to fall back on. Some children do not have necessaries of life. Recommends not turning loose all at once; allow young people who finish education to have property turned over.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Cantonment Agency, Eagle City Oklahoma
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on condition of fee patent Indians
testimony.subject: Condition of Cheyenne and Arapahoe fee patent Indians
testimony.key_claims: Worked in Government service three years with Cheyenne and Arapahoe Indians. Only a few have kept land after receiving patent; nearly all sell as soon as they can and run through money but are satisfied and go to work and make better citizens. Named Indians with land under Government control making success of farming: David Bighead, Harry Bates, Walter Fire, Dan Tucker. Named 13 Indians living about Avery and Cushing Oklahoma who sold land after receiving patents. Recommends allowing disposal of heired lands while holding own allotments; portion of miners' interests in heired lands to be deposited and draw interest until of age.

testimony.witness_title: Superintendent, Spokane Indian Agency, Wellpinit Washington
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on condition of fee patent Indians
testimony.subject: Fee patents to Spokane Indians; releasing Indians from Government supervision
testimony.key_claims: 112 Indians received fee patents for original allotments. Patents issued 1910-1921. 54 fee patent Indians retained original allotments; 48 sold. Most of 54 retaining are farming own lands; few women leasing. Condition of those who sold is as good as when they held lands. Cannot recall that any are dissatisfied. Does not believe Indians of Spokane Reservation released too soon. Spokane allotments mostly 80 acres or less, mostly timber not valuable, not worth more than $400-$800 after timber cut. Does not think good policy to make all Indians full citizens at once based on blood quantum; each case should be decided on its merits considering education, business experience, degree of blood, robustness, and age. Recommends holding 20 to 40 acres in trust for homesite.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Spokane Indian Agency, Wellpinit Washington
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on condition of fee patent Indians
testimony.subject: Condition of fee patent Indians on Spokane Reservation
testimony.key_claims: Larger percent of fee patent Indians on Spokane Reservation doing as well as before Government control. Most satisfied with receiving patents. Larger percent of those who sold used money to good advantage. Would examine each case individually. Names of those who sold and are getting along: Del Brown (Miles WA - renting place, interest in sawmill), Caulette Ford (Chewelah WA - built house), Albert Sochemtioken/Garry (Wellpinit WA - sold for $3000 and auto, spent money but has $1000 due and still has car, good worker), Daniel Sherwood (Wellpinit WA - bought better place), Duncan Desautel (Lincoln WA - sold and lived up money but making good living). Those still holding land: John Inkster Jr. (Ford WA - renting allotments of two old Indians, good farming).

testimony.witness_title: Field Clerk, United States Indian Service, Poteau Oklahoma
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on condition of fee patent Indians
testimony.subject: Full removal of restrictions from Choctaw Indians and Five Tribes
testimony.key_claims: Government's work in Five Tribes has been to divide tribes' common estate and vest in each Indian his proportionate share. Blood quantum alone should not determine management of individual case. Considers character, education especially business experience, degree of blood, robustness, age, and circumstances. Many should have restrictions retained indefinitely especially those in out-of-the-way places retaining old tribal customs. Considerable number are reasonably competent. Between 50 and 75 percent have made a success. Most failures come from easy money - Indian regards freedom as windfall of ready cash rather than life responsibility. Drink usually plays big part in failures. Dependents of allottee should weigh heavily in decision. Believes best that 20 to 40 acres be held in trust for homesite. Recommends removing restrictions from inherited land as soon as heirs determined.

testimony.witness_title: Superintendent, Kiowa Indian Agency, Anadarko Oklahoma
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on condition of fee patent Indians
testimony.subject: Patents-in-fee at Kiowa Indian Agency; administrative policy on issuance
testimony.key_claims: Most important administrative function of Indian superintendent is deciding whether to recommend favorably on application for patent-in-fee. Granting patent prematurely subjects Indian to temptation to dissipate estate and acquire extravagant habits. Withholding patent from competent Indian robs him of experience. Always felt it better to err by delaying patent than granting too soon. Does not think good policy to issue patents based on blood quantum or educational qualifications alone. Has full-blood Indians who cannot speak English who are more competent than some with small Indian blood. Of last 60 patents issued under Declaration of Policy: 20 promptly mortgaged (only 1 released), 16 sold outright, 24 so far clear. In 6+ years cannot recall but one case where Indian made a success handling land, and that success could have been achieved under trust. Proposes Government make every Indian select 40 acres as inalienable homestead by Act of Congress, taxable after trust period but taxes not collectable from that property. Allows inherited land restrictions to be removed as heirs determined. Does not believe there are half a dozen of several hundred patents granted who are as competent as average white man.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, United States Indian Service
testimony.hearing: Patent-in-fee questionnaire response
testimony.committee: Board of Indian Commissioners / Office of Indian Affairs
testimony.subject: Issuance of patents-in-fee; outcomes for Indian allottees
testimony.key_claims: Of last sixty patents issued under Declaration of Policy, twenty promptly mortgaged (only one released), sixteen sold outright, twenty-four technically clear but expected to become encumbered. In six-plus years, only one Indian made success handling his own land, and that success could have been made under trust. Does not recall even one case of genuine success. Opposes easy issuance of patents. Advocates making forty acres of each allotment an inalienable homestead. Indians allotted 160 acres each. Knows of no Indian who has more land now than when allotted. Described loan agent inquiry about Billy Hood's patent and agent's attempt to negotiate loan in anticipation of patent. In about 99 out of 100 cases, patent is never asked for until applicant has studied out a plan to alienate it.

testimony.witness_title: Acting Field Clerk, Tahlequah, Oklahoma (Five Civilized Tribes / Cherokee)
testimony.hearing: Response to Field Division letter of April 2, 1921
testimony.committee: Board of Indian Commissioners / Office of Indian Affairs
testimony.subject: Advisability of granting patents-in-fee; outcomes for Five Civilized Tribes Indians
testimony.key_claims: Indiscriminate policy of releasing every Indian of half or less blood degree without supervision is criminally unjust and disastrously impractical. Of those released through competency board, approximately 10% failed completely, 10% barely escape failure, 50% succeeding indifferently, 30% making decided success. Ten percent of those whose restrictions were removed by careful selection sold lands and misused proceeds; remaining 90% made good. Competent Indians rarely apply for removal of restrictions because restricted land is not subject to taxation and they value their homes. Full-blood Indians do not realise value of money. Success correlated with education. Impossible to apply hard and fast rule to all Indians alike. Has worked only with Five Civilized Tribes for six to seven years. Advocates competency board process over indiscriminate release.

testimony.witness_title: tribal member, unnamed reservation
testimony.hearing: Patent-in-fee questionnaire / opinion submission
testimony.committee: Board of Indian Commissioners / Office of Indian Affairs
testimony.subject: Opposition to rapid release from federal control and indiscriminate citizenship granting
testimony.key_claims: Over 500 Indians on reservation released from government control; very few made good, others sold lands and homes and squandered money, some homeless. Opposed to societies advocating abolition of Indian Bureau. Opposed to granting citizenship in bulk. Contends Department moving too fast in releasing Indians. Advocates competent Indians classifying reservation members in harmony with superintendent, with rigid examination of every Indian regardless of blood or educational status before release. Where Indian has established home, forty acres should be held in trust, nontaxable for given period. Majority of ex-Indian soldiers without lands and not independent citizens. Act of Congress March 2, 1889 provided allotments. American Legion says ex-Indian soldiers should be citizens.

testimony.witness_title: Indian Superintendent, unnamed agency
testimony.hearing: Patent-in-fee questionnaire response
testimony.committee: Board of Indian Commissioners / Office of Indian Affairs
testimony.subject: Criteria for competency; outcomes of patent issuance; reimbursable agreements
testimony.key_claims: Many different ideas of competency exist among superintendents: commercial success, likelihood of running through property, or education. Department has not provided clear guidance; superintendents believe Department desires rapid patent issuance but burden of responsibility falls on superintendent. Several hundred patents granted at reservation; does not believe half dozen of entire number resulted in Indians being as competent as average white man. First generation since allotting ran through more than half land holdings. If land held in trust, Indians have good prospect of becoming worthy citizens; if turned loose most would become parasites. Patents generally theoretically assume patentee has sufficient knowledge and business foresight. Reimbursable plan, if properly handled, would help Indians. Advocates more schooling, mission work, better superintendents. Competent Indian never makes application for removal of restrictions. At competency commission hearings, those who asked for patents were not nearly as qualified as those who did not.

testimony.witness_title: Field Clerk, Okmulgee, Oklahoma, Five Civilized Tribes; enrolled member Chickasaw tribe
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on releasing Indians from Government supervision
testimony.subject: Releasing Indians from Government supervision; restriction policy; land sales; education
testimony.key_claims: 30% of Indians under his supervision given freedom from Government control are making decided success; 50% succeeding indifferently well; 10% barely escape failure; 10% have failed completely. Competent Indians rarely apply for removal of restrictions because restricted land is non-taxable and they value their homes. 10% of those whose restrictions were removed by competency commission have sold their lands and misused proceeds; 90% have made good. Full-blood Indians enrolled as less than full-blood due to enrollment irregularities. Education is the only solution. Opposes both total removal of restrictions and keeping all restricted. Supports middle course. Proposes Secretary of Interior approval for conveyance of deceased allottees' lands. Members of Five Civilized Tribes served in World War I financially and with lives.

testimony.witness_title: Field Clerk, Holdenville, Oklahoma, Five Civilized Tribes
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on releasing Indians from Government supervision
testimony.subject: Releasing Indians from Government supervision; restriction removal; inherited lands; taxation; guardianship; leasing
testimony.key_claims: Very small percentage of fully released Indians in his district are making a success. At least 75% of those whose restrictions removed have disposed of their allotments. When restriction removal order becomes effective, Indians proceed to sell land or encumber it with loans. Purchasers secure loans from loan companies in excess of purchase price. Indians inexperienced with taxes leave them unpaid; penalties accrue; tax deeds issued. At least 90% of allottees lease surplus land for cash in advance at fraction of real value; money soon spent; allottee left without support, becomes idler. Inherited lands revealed upon examination to be 75% or more sold for 50% or less of real value. Probate court sales inadequately supervised; US probate attorneys' protests ignored. Proposes legislation requiring appraisal and advertisement for inherited land sales, impounding proceeds. Proposes Congress require all lease contracts under field clerk supervision. Proposes compulsory retention of 40 acres homestead.

testimony.witness_title: Field Clerk, Ardmore, Oklahoma, Five Civilized Tribes
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on releasing Indians from Government supervision
testimony.subject: Patent-in-fee policy; merit-based restriction removal; reservation of homestead land
testimony.key_claims: Policy of granting patents-in-fee has been premature in many cases; trust created by Congress has not been kept as intended; injury rather than good has resulted. Matter of removal of restrictions should be decided on merits not quantum of Indian blood. Many less-than-half-bloods less fit than full-bloods. Too much liberality in general removal of restrictions from less-than-half-bloods has made them prey of designing, resourceful men. Would reserve 40 acres of average land restricted until death as homestead, also becoming heritage to heirs born after tribal rolls closed. Believes much damage has been done that would have been avoided with earlier action. In his opinion only small percent have made full success after restriction removal; majority not going forward as hoped.

testimony.witness_title: Superintendent, Crow Indian Reservation, Crow Agency, Montana
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on releasing Indians from Government supervision
testimony.subject: Releasing Crow Indians from Government supervision; patent-in-fee conditions
testimony.key_claims: Compiled tabular statement showing data on patent-in-fee Indians. Has little to add to letters from field matron and farmers, especially missionary whose views align closely with his own. Wrote to all farmers, field matrons, and missionaries after receiving March 31, 1921 circular. Had hoped for report from Father Taelman who worked among Indians long time but not received. Believes individual allotments should be given with responsibility forced upon Indians, not nurtured; younger people with schooling should receive their portion and learn consequences of indolence.

testimony.witness_title: Baptist Missionary, Crow Reservation, Montana
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on releasing Indians from Government supervision
testimony.subject: Releasing Indians from Government supervision
testimony.key_claims: Letter described by Asbury as not sentimental but cold-blooded; views nearly identical to Asbury's own opinion. Has charge of extensive missionary work including community and school activities. Believes Indians must be put on their own responsibility and this cannot be achieved through nursing but must be forced upon them.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Lodge Grass, Crow Reservation, Montana
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on releasing Indians from Government supervision
testimony.subject: Releasing Indians from Government supervision on Crow Reservation
testimony.key_claims: Goes into subject quite fully according to Asbury. Describes situation at Lodge Grass. Asbury commends letter for careful consideration as Cope has been employed on reservation for number of years and is man of intelligence thoroughly interested in real Indian progress.

testimony.witness_title: Field Matron, St. Xavier, Crow Reservation, Montana
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on releasing Indians from Government supervision
testimony.subject: Releasing Indians from Government supervision
testimony.key_claims: Has been employed on reservation in many capacities for many years; woman of intelligence interested in progress of Indian; opinion should carry considerable weight according to Asbury.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Wyola, Crow Reservation, Montana
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on releasing Indians from Government supervision
testimony.subject: Situation regarding releasing Indians from Government supervision on Crow Reservation
testimony.key_claims: Covers the situation rather briefly per Asbury's description.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Crow Reservation, Wyola, Montana
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on patent-in-fee policy
testimony.committee: Board of Indian Commissioners / Office of Indian Affairs
testimony.subject: Condition of fee patent Indians on Crow Reservation
testimony.key_claims: Most fee patent Indians are getting an expensive lesson in experience. Financially, the majority are in a worse condition than before receiving patents. 95% of Crow Indians given full control of property would be paupers in less than three years. Fee patent Indians he knows cannot compete with the average white man. Recommends thorough examination before releasing Indians from Government control.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Crow Reservation, Lodge Grass, Montana
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on patent-in-fee policy
testimony.committee: Board of Indian Commissioners / Office of Indian Affairs
testimony.subject: Patent-in-fee policy for Crow Indians; best policy for releasing Indians from Government control
testimony.key_claims: Government is going too fast in releasing Indians; percentage who made good is considerably smaller than those who failed. Fee patent Indians have mortgaged land, speculated unwisely, or living in ease. Indian's business experience with white men always results in the Indian losing money. Chances of success for today's Indians are very small without practical training. Should not release homestead part of allotment; keep it inalienable. Would give patents to capable individuals regardless of whether they speak English; full-bloods are more capable and dependable than mixed-bloods. Fee patent Indian who has sold all property and spent money unwisely is invariably the greatest agitator.

testimony.witness_title: Field Matron, Crow Reservation, St. Xavier, Montana
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on patent-in-fee policy
testimony.committee: Board of Indian Commissioners / Office of Indian Affairs
testimony.subject: Individual case outcomes for fee patent Indians on Crow Reservation
testimony.key_claims: Joseph Cooper obtained patent, sold land, now in tent farming agency land. Henry Reid sold land, bought automobile, home on wife's land. Ralph Saco sold land, bought high-priced auto, lost car and land. Ben Gardner sold land near oil well for enough to buy a Ford, lives in cabin on wife's land. Mrs. Mary Takes The Gun has not sold land; her husband runs cattle. Mrs. Amy Scott had ideal cattle ranch, secured mortgage, bought and mortgaged cattle, eventually lost everything. Oldest son sold land; second son has land mortgaged to limit near oil well. Mrs. Olive R. Venne mortgaged home, bought auto, motor truck, engine; items mortgaged and some sold at sheriff's sale. Two unnamed Indians who recently died had mortgaged places - both considered very capable. Mrs. Mary Humphrey benefited from citizenship. Thomas LaForge has patent but has sold no land. Richard Wallace does not want a patent. In majority of cases Indians are worse off since receiving patents.

testimony.witness_title: Baptist Missionary, Lodge Grass, Crow Reservation, Montana
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on patent-in-fee policy
testimony.committee: Board of Indian Commissioners / Office of Indian Affairs
testimony.subject: Policy on releasing Indians from Government supervision
testimony.key_claims: Not personally in favor of turning all Indians loose at once. Most Indians will not amount to anything until they have exhausted what is given to them and then will begin to climb. It is wrong policy to hold capable Indians as Government wards. Indian has right to be a prodigal son and should learn from bitter experience not be kept out of school of hard knocks. Old Indians should remain wards. Some comparatively well-to-do part-blood Crows refused citizenship to avoid taxes and get Indian office help. Some Indians should be forced to accept citizenship. Citizenship should be conferred as soon as possible on all except old Indians and a few others. Richard Wallace is one of most progressive Indians but believes in Government control. Few fee patent Indians in district holding land and farming. Most Crows with patents do not make good use of land or money. Speed of Indian Office shrinkage policy is debatable.

testimony.witness_title: Superintendent, Crow Indian Reservation, Crow Agency, Montana
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on patent-in-fee policy
testimony.committee: Board of Indian Commissioners / Office of Indian Affairs
testimony.subject: Compilation of data on patent-in-fee Indians at Crow Reservation
testimony.key_claims: Out of 301 Indians, reports made on disposition of property of 140. Of 140: 54 held land (10 had mortgages), 84 (60%) sold all land, 2 sold part. Condition of 105 patent-in-fee Crows: 8 good/fair, 9 same, 39 worse/poor. Land money use of 77: 13 farming/stock/land/investments, 35 business venture/living expenses/payment on mortgage and lawyer's fee, 5 indifferent, 13 squandered on luxuries and automobiles. Occupation of 82: 8 farming or ranching, 17 farming some, 5 laborers, 13 Government/Army/Navy, 8 doing very little or nothing, 17 miscellaneous. Agrees with Cope and Petzoldt's letters. Recommends not adopting wholesale policy but giving capable individuals their allotments and capitalizing tribal property. Does not believe wholesale release should result in suffering among old people. Advocates Section 13 of Crow Allotment Act as beneficial.

testimony.witness_title: Field Clerk, United States Indian Service, Tulsa, Oklahoma
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on patent-in-fee policy
testimony.committee: Board of Indian Commissioners / Office of Indian Affairs
testimony.subject: Fee patent Indians in Tulsa, Creek, Cherokee and Washington counties, Oklahoma
testimony.key_claims: Practically all half-bloods in these counties have been turned loose. About 100 Indians of more than half-blood turned loose through competency commissions, about 25 through departmental process. Large percent of latter made good use of property; more successful in retaining property than average white man. Half-bloods in Five Tribes had all restrictions on surplus allotments removed by Act of Congress; very small percent retained lands. Stresses worker's ability and disposition over schooling in recommending removal. Educated Indian not necessarily more successful than worker who cannot read or write. Not in favor of blanket removals. Young man leaving eighth grade not better prepared than a proven worker. Ability of Indians to conduct own business is not being shown. Few fee patent Indians in district holding lands and farming.

testimony.witness_title: Field Clerk, United States Indian Service, Choctaw and Chickasaw Indians, Durant, Oklahoma
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on patent-in-fee policy
testimony.committee: Board of Indian Commissioners / Office of Indian Affairs
testimony.subject: Indian affairs, patent-in-fee policy, Five Civilized Tribes vs. reservation Indians
testimony.key_claims: Acknowledges April 2, 1921 communication. Intention of Department is for betterment of the race but red tape and theoretical methods have made more Indians dependent than necessary. No distinction made between various tribes is a mistake - Five Civilized Tribes are as different from reservation Indians as Caucasian from Mexican. Five Tribes were never known to rebel against U.S. Government; their members follow every vocation known to white man. Indians should be dealt with as individuals not as a race. About 60% of Indians released by competency commission from Five Tribes sold or mortgaged property; about 80% went to work and became good citizens. Better citizen without land if he works after selling it. Criticized bureaucratic inefficiency: field clerk at $1800/year, superintendent's transmitting clerk at $1500/year, Washington clerk at only $1200/year doing final approval. Congressman investigated this discrepancy. Oklahoma Congressman noted field clerk was more competent than Washington clerk. Recommends: able-bodied Indians with eighth-grade education aged 21-35 should get unconditional removal of all restrictions; homestead of 40 acres should be protected. Restrictions on Five Tribes land to be automatically removed in 1931; need protection for incompetent Indians before then. Has lived among Indians all his life.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, United States Indian Service, Shawnee Agency, Oklahoma
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on patent-in-fee policy
testimony.committee: Board of Indian Commissioners / Office of Indian Affairs
testimony.subject: Patent-in-fee policy; Mack Johnson case; Indian at Shawnee Agency
testimony.key_claims: Supplementing earlier letter. Mack Johnson, Kickapoo, was given patent to 40 acres of good bottom land worth $3000-$4000; land slipped away and money gone in short time; also had mortgage still pending on team, tools, stock. A separate unnamed Indian mortgaged his stuff, took money to Mexico, died there leaving wife and small children destitute; missionary and white neighbors now providing food. That Indian blamed the agent who recommended his patent for putting him out of business; the agent had more experience and foresight but the people lost confidence in him. An Indian who asked for his patent and had it recommended - before he realized it, his land was gone. Agent who recommended patent without sufficient reason was responsible in larger sense for the condition. Recommends protecting homestead of 40 acres, not allowing leasing of that portion. 95% of Crow Indians given full control would be paupers in three years. Believes majority of Indians who sell land do go to work. Rule cannot be applied to all - old Indians and minor children must be protected.

testimony.witness_title: Superintendent, Fort Peck Indian Reservation (formerly Standing Rock, North Dakota)
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on patent-in-fee policy
testimony.committee: Board of Indian Commissioners / Office of Indian Affairs
testimony.subject: Patent-in-fee experience at Standing Rock Reservation, North Dakota
testimony.key_claims: Was on special detail purchasing cattle in southwest before being transferred to Fort Peck. Approximately 600 patents-in-fee issued at Standing Rock beginning prior to 1915 with mixed-bloods and educated Indians. Very few original recipients failed Government's purpose; many acquired homes and this issue was a benefit. Next issuance in 1916 dealt largely with mixed-blood element as competent as white people but practically all this land was disposed of; many women married to white men immediately disposed of lands. Subsequent Competency Commission dealt with those regardless of blood who had been successful in industrial work; returned soldiers issued patents - fair percentage retained lands. Children of 1908-1909 allotted land 50-70 miles from parents' homes under Enabling Act of 1905; many of these young people sold allotments not because they were spendthrifts but because the land was of no use to them; money was often wisely spent on cattle, implements, improvements on land where they actually lived. Young industrious Indians who sold distant allotments should not be judged harshly. Mixed-blood women married to white men disposed of lands immediately.

testimony.witness: unnamed correspondent (formerly at Standing Rock, North Dakota)
testimony.witness_title: Former agent/superintendent at Standing Rock, transferred to Fort Peck
testimony.hearing: response to circular letter
testimony.subject: Outcomes of fee patent policy at Standing Rock Reservation
testimony.key_claims: Fee patents dealt largely with mixed-blood element, practically all as educated and competent as white people, but practically all land was disposed of. Mortgages and interest ate up resources. Only one Indian known to have regained his allotment. Subsequent issues by Competency Commission dealt with those successful in industrial work and returned soldiers; fair percentage retained lands. Young Indians allotted land 50-70 miles from parents' homes had little use for allotments. Money was in many cases wisely spent on cattle and implements. Inheritance of multiple scattered allotments made consolidation nearly impossible. County land speculators used unethical practices to induce land sales. Issuance of patents was a benefit as it gave Indians independence and self-determination.

testimony.witness_title: Superintendent, Cheyenne River Agency, South Dakota
testimony.hearing: response to circular letter
testimony.subject: Fee patent policy outcomes at Cheyenne River Agency and general Indian land policy
testimony.key_claims: Standing Rock Reservation originally over three million acres; allotments ranged from 160 acres (unmarried) to 640 acres (heads of families) to 320 acres (wives). Most valuable agricultural land allotted to children whose families were miles away due to railroad building. Many young Indians sold allotments simply because land was too remote to use. Money often wisely spent on cattle and improvements. Inheritance of scattered allotments made use impossible. Strongly opposed to allowing Indians to lease home allotment. Believes fee patent issuance should continue on individual merit basis, not class distinction. Most successful citizen Indians on Standing Rock are those of more than one-half Indian blood. At Pine Ridge, April 1918: 341 patents issued to those with less than one-half Indian blood; September 1919: 370 patents to those of half or less blood. About 10% retained lands free of debt; 15% more have equity with mortgages of half to two-thirds value; majority sold and are now living on relatives. Tendency of Indians to convert land to cash as quickly as possible. Issuing patents indiscriminately would be disastrous.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Cheyenne River Agency, Promise, South Dakota
testimony.hearing: response to circular letter
testimony.subject: Fee patent Indian conditions in his district
testimony.key_claims: Government released Indians from federal control too suddenly. Some were made citizens under protest. Majority of first fee patent Indians sold all their lands and spent the money. Those who sold deliberately are in worse condition. Recommends individual examination of each case and sending government machinery free of charge to assist remaining Indian landowners. County authorities assessed allotted grazing lands as farm lands causing high taxes. Original ruling was allottee holds land for 25 years then receives patent if capable, or 10-year extension; county overrules this. Every head of family allotted 640 acres as grazing land. Tax burden shocked Indians and made them want to rid themselves of patents.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Cheyenne River Agency, Whitehorse, South Dakota
testimony.hearing: response to circular letter
testimony.subject: Fee patent Indian policy at Cheyenne River Agency Whitehouse District
testimony.key_claims: Out of 57 citizen Indians in Whitehouse District, 45 have sold their lands and 12 are holding. High percent of those who disposed of lands have little to show for sale money. Young Indian using white man as example in everyday habits and getting same education advantages. Experience will be his teacher and younger he gets it the sooner he will realize his worth. Old Indians must be protected. Some have used money to make improvements on homes. Recommends giving each Indian individual chance and making him care for himself.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Pine Ridge Reservation, Eagle Nest District, Wanblee, South Dakota
testimony.hearing: response to circular letter
testimony.subject: Fee patent Indian conditions and policy recommendations at Eagle Nest District
testimony.key_claims: Most successful citizen Indians on Standing Rock are those of more than one-half Indian blood. Does not agree degree of blood is measure of competency. Each case should be on individual merit. 90% of unmarried Indians allotted land miles from homes with no practical use for allotments. Leases and sales were only method of remuneration. Fee patent issuance was benefit - Indians now feel independent and self-reliant. Believes policy of issuing fee patents to competent Indians should continue so children of these Indians learn to feel proper responsibility. Believes each case should be judged individually, not by blood or class distinction.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Pine Ridge Indian Reservation, Anderson, South Dakota
testimony.hearing: response to circular letter
testimony.subject: Fee patent Indian conditions at Pine Ridge
testimony.key_claims: About one-fourth of those turned loose have sold none of their land and are accumulating property. About one-fourth have sold part and used money for stock and machinery. About one-half have sold lands with very little to show for proceeds. Recommends individual case-by-case assessment. Believes Indians should be compelled to retain 160 acres under trust. Withholding patents at present time recommended as land prices are low and not equal to appraised valuation. Few cases where patent-in-fee Indians are really better off financially.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Pine Ridge Reservation, Oglala, South Dakota
testimony.hearing: response to circular letter
testimony.subject: Fee patent Indian outcomes with case examples of Leroy Cuny and William Twiss
testimony.key_claims: As soon as Indian receives patent-in-fee he tries to sell land for cash and stock. If cannot sell he mortgages it. Government not handling releasing of Indians correctly. Only policy is to take each case individually. Leroy Cuny, 39 years old, declared citizen, disposed of none of his land, raised large family, has 300 head of cattle, horses, hogs, poultry, making money, farming on large scale. William Twiss, 58 years old, cannot read, only writes name, immediately disposed of all land and has absolutely nothing to show for it, people caring for his children. Has been a little too fast in some cases turning Indians loose. Recommends each Indian be compelled to retain 160 acres under trust. Ten to twenty acres as homestead would amount to very little.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Pine Ridge Indian Reservation, Wakpamni District, Pine Ridge, South Dakota
testimony.hearing: response to circular letter
testimony.subject: Fee patent Indian conditions at Wakpamni District, Pine Ridge
testimony.key_claims: Wishes to state that with exception of three Indians, all who received patents-in-fee in his district are in much worse condition than before release from federal control. Three exceptions have not sold their land, have small herds of cattle, farming on small scale, contented and happy. All others sold allotments and spent money on automobiles and riotous living. Generally dissatisfied and seeking more money from Government. Recommends releasing all young able-bodied educated Indians from federal control; allowing others to sell part of allotment holding quarter section as homesite; money from sales held in trust and expenditure supervised by superintendent.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Pine Ridge Indian Reservation, Porcupine, South Dakota
testimony.hearing: response to circular letter
testimony.subject: Fee patent Indian outcomes at Porcupine District
testimony.key_claims: Does not know of any patent-in-fee Indians who have made good from land sales. Quite a number have done exceedingly well and others have done nothing; receiving patents has been great detriment. Those turned loose seem satisfied with what has been done for them. A few retained all land and making good, but only small number, and these were doing well before patents were issued. Some sold part of land and improved homes. Others sold and have nothing. Some who are competent say only reason they do not apply for patents is they do not want to pay taxes. Recommends handling each case separately. In some cases retaining homestead would be detriment as Indian would think it made no difference what happened to rest of land.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Pine Ridge Indian Reservation, Kyle, South Dakota
testimony.hearing: response to circular letter
testimony.subject: Fee patent Indian policy at Kyle District
testimony.key_claims: Will not say Government is too fast in releasing Indians. Recommends individual examination of each case by superintendent and farmers. Some who are competent refuse to apply for patents to avoid paying taxes. Recommends looking into each case separately. Not much difference made between land character and Indian character in assessing policy.

testimony.witness_title: Superintendent, Shoshone Indian Reservation, Fort Washakie, Wyoming
testimony.hearing: response to circular letter
testimony.subject: Statistical and qualitative outcomes of fee patent policy at Shoshone Indian Reservation
testimony.key_claims: 303 patents-in-fee issued at Shoshone Reservation 1907-1930. Breakdown: 1907:1, 1909:3, 1910:2, 1911:5, 1912:2, 1913:3, 1914:7, 1915:9, 1916:41, 1917:3, 1918:8, 1919:85, 1930(sic):34, total 303. Blood group breakdown provided. About 90% have either sold or mortgaged lands. Some few made beneficial use of proceeds purchasing livestock and agricultural equipment. Majority squandered lands in extravagant living and purchase of automobiles. Those who went broke have settled down to work for wages making better showing. Patent Indians mostly half-blood or less, educated, speak English fluently, in prime of life. Doubts single instance on reservation where if patent-in-fee Indians removed they would not make better showing. Reservation environment is great drawback. Favors entire removal of restrictions where Indians deemed competent. Recommends holding back not less than 160 acres as reservation not adapted for farming. Great caution in granting patents. Ignorant full-blood may be as competent as educated breed who is indolent. Industrial education in schools is of first importance.

testimony.witness: unnamed superintendent (formerly at Standing Rock, responding about general policy)
testimony.witness_title: Superintendent (unidentified, Pine Ridge area context)
testimony.hearing: response to circular letter
testimony.subject: General policy on fee patents and Indian citizenship
testimony.key_claims: Does not believe disposition or sale of Indian allotments is proper basis for judging success of policy. Does not agree that Indian must be pauperized to get proper start. Does not believe any land should be retained in trust as it removes responsibility from Indian. Believes issuance of patents and freeing from jurisdictional control has been benefit to Indians involved. Each individual Indian has a natural sphere or level they will attain. Unscrupulous white men including so-called bankers and land speculators used unethical practices to induce land sales. Indians suddenly thrown on own resources and subject to desire for money came under influence of unscrupulous white men. Indian same as white person has a certain sphere of physical and mental attainment.

testimony.witness_title: Superintendent, Shoshone Indian Reservation
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners Survey - Bulletin No. 138
testimony.subject: Results of fee patents at Shoshone Indian Reservation
testimony.key_claims: 303 fee patents issued 1907-1930 at Shoshone Reservation averaging 80 acres of good irrigable agricultural land. Approximately 90% of recipients either sold or mortgaged their lands. Some few made beneficial use of proceeds through purchase of livestock and agricultural equipment. Recommends against issuing patents without individual examination and recommends holding back not less than 160 acres as the reservation is not adapted for farming. Cautions against granting patents to females as their property is soon squandered by husbands, desertions are frequent, and women are left with small children without means of support.

testimony.witness_title: Superintendent, Cheyenne & Arapaho Indian Agency
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners Survey - Bulletin No. 138
testimony.subject: Effects of releasing Indians from Government control at Cheyenne & Arapaho Agency
testimony.key_claims: In practically every case lands have been sold. A great many used proceeds unwisely; possibly a majority used proceeds for improvement of other family lands or investment in other business. Believes beneficial to give able-bodied competent Indians their patents. Recommends examining each individual case as to age, opportunity and physical capacity. After Indian receives patent, agency officials do not follow up their activities and Indians resent any effort to find out what they are doing with lands or proceeds. Agency officials often have only general knowledge of consequences of patents. Notes Indians frequently say the Government turned them loose and see no reason for further oversight.

testimony.witness_title: Superintendent, Yankton Indian Agency
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners Survey - Bulletin No. 138
testimony.subject: Results of 613 fee patents at Yankton Sioux Reservation
testimony.key_claims: 599 full allotment patents and 13 partial issued. Originally 3113 allotments comprising 368,400 acres on reservation. Approximately half of patents issued prior to 1916, some by special Act of Congress. Secretary of Interior visited in May 1916 and delivered 186 patents based on Competency Commission report. About 100 more issued under Declaration of Policy. Not to exceed 10 of 613 recipients own entire original allotment; perhaps not to exceed 50 own any portion. Approximately 550 have disposed of all land; approximately 400 have absolutely nothing to show. Only 59,000 acres remain in trust. Allotments ranged 80-320 acres; heads of families received 160 acres agricultural or 320 acres grazing; minors received 80 acres agricultural or 160 acres grazing; full-bloods received 60 acres. Mixed-bloods used sharp practice to have allotments classified as grazing land to obtain twice the acreage. About 80% of reservation land is excellent agricultural land. Indians typically dispose of land almost immediately after receiving patents, usually within 12 months. Primary means of squandering: purchase of automobiles, beset by white men at below-adequate prices. Approximately 60% of able-bodied members farm to some extent. Recommends either refuse to issue patents to any part of allotments or issue to all; no partial releases.

testimony.witness_title: United States Indian Farmer, Yankton Indian Reservation
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners Survey - Bulletin No. 138
testimony.subject: Views on releasing Santee and Yankton Sioux from Government supervision based on field experience
testimony.key_claims: Does not advocate turning Indians loose irrespective of qualifications but believes each case should receive careful consideration. Every young able-bodied Indian whose mind is functioning properly should have everything turned over unrestricted. Does not believe in reserving part of allotment as safety net. Indian should either be full citizen or ward with no compromise. Young Indians who are not able-bodied or weak-minded, and all old and indigent ones, should remain under supervision. Many will squander everything in a year or two but if still able to work they will make better citizens. Cites Joseph Ellis and Thomas Hunter of Lake Andes, and Robert Medicinehorn and Mark Patterson of Watertown area as examples of successful fee patent holders among Yankton Sioux. Cites Simon Vasser and Gilbert St. Pierre of Wagner as other examples.

testimony.witness_title: Superintendent, Rosebud Indian Agency
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners Survey - Bulletin No. 138
testimony.subject: Policy on patents-in-fee and competency at Rosebud Agency
testimony.key_claims: Approximately 600 fee patents issued under this agency, records not kept up to date. About 90% of patent recipients immediately sold allotments or mortgaged and sold when mortgage came due. 85% of allotments were 160 acres, ranging in value from $1000 to $16,000 with average of about $4000 per quarter section. Opposes granting patents in bulk; every case should be decided on its merits irrespective of blood status or educational qualifications. An Indian can be competent to earn a living but not competent to manage $10,000-$15,000 property. Not to exceed one Indian in ten who receives patent uses proceeds for productive purposes such as teams, farm implements, or home improvements. Recommends Office outline a standard for Competency Commissioner and Superintendents to follow. Indian should be given full control of property without governmental supervision when competent but not before.

testimony.witness_title: Superintendent, Rosebud Indian Agency
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on fee patent policy
testimony.subject: Effect of fee patent policy on Rosebud Sioux; approximately 600 out of 5,500 received patents-in-fee
testimony.key_claims: About 90% of Indians receiving patents-in-fee sold their land immediately; 9 out of 10 sold land and spent proceeds within 1-2 years; nearly all bought a car after land was sold; upkeep of cars consumed most funds; not more than 1 in 10 used money for productive purposes; allotment values ranged $1,000-$16,000 averaging $4,000 per 160-acre quarter; recommended individual competency assessment not bulk issuance; advocated for full control given only when genuinely competent; suggested standardized criteria for Competency Commissioners

testimony.witness_title: Superintendent, Turtle Mountain Indian Agency
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on fee patent policy
testimony.subject: Effect of fee patent policy on Turtle Mountain Indians; tabulation of 1,393 patents issued 1910-1921
testimony.key_claims: Government has gone too swiftly in issuing patents-in-fee; fully 95% sold their land as soon as they received patent; if mortgage placed on land, Indians made no sincere effort to repay, not even interest and taxes paid; not over 5% of fee patent Indians holding original allotments; those holding land are farming it themselves; taxes on Indian reservations are high and exceed income from land; better business proposition to let land remain as trust and lease it; land values in Montana and western North Dakota have slumped badly; majority wanting to dispose of land should petition as incompetent; future patents should only go to those likely to prove equal of white neighbors; scrutiny should be based on character, experience, and intelligence not blood status

testimony.witness_title: Agency Farmer, Turtle Mountain Agency
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on fee patent policy
testimony.subject: Effect of fee patent policy; condition of patent-in-fee Indians at Turtle Mountain
testimony.key_claims: General impression that Indians are being released from federal supervision too rapidly; inability to handle large tracts of land on paying basis; inability to compete with experienced white businessmen placed citizen Indian at great disadvantage resulting in great loss; nearly all patent-in-fee Indians worse off now than when they became independent citizens; many sold land at first opportunity regardless of price; others anxious to sell and spend proceeds; progressive Indian dissatisfied with what received; realized compelled to bear taxation burden; does not believe they were greatly benefitted; well-to-do Indians refused patents; named examples of those doing well and doing poorly; recommended modified merit system based on industry, honesty, and economy; at least one-half of any valuable allotment should be held in trust as home site for lifetime of Indian

testimony.witness_title: Superintendent, LaPointe Indian Agency
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on fee patent policy
testimony.subject: Fee patent outcomes at Bad River Reservation; 373 certificates of competency issued 1913-1921
testimony.key_claims: Presumes 98% of 373 Indians granted certificates of competency sold their land; does not know of any patent-in-fee Indian who has not sold all or most of land; restricted fee patents not trust patents issued to local Indians; law on arbitrary issuance to half-blood or less does not apply to Bad River Reservation; granting of certificates made purely personal proposition; some sold money fast and are now broke working; others invested proceeds wisely; Indians are just like other people in business capacity; Indian generally less frugal than white brother; local allotments 80 acres each; cut-over land not in active demand; prices ranged $300-$1,500 mostly under $500; funds not large enough to markedly change financial status; aged full-blood ignorant class and minors should still be guarded; modern educated Bad River Chippewa should be turned loose; parents declared competent asking for minor childrens funds; about 150 Indians employed at saw mill; about one million dollars still held for aged and minors

testimony.witness_title: Superintendent, Nez Perce Indian Agency
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on fee patent policy
testimony.subject: Effect of fee patent policy on Nez Perce; approximately 500 fee patents issued; analysis of generational differences in land management
testimony.key_claims: About 500 fee patents issued to Nez Perces total; prima facie competent (young educated class) are first to dispose of lands and squander proceeds; older people grew up having to work and save, hold onto land and save money; full-blood Nez Perce woman who cannot read write or speak English holds $13,000 mortgage on 480 acres of white man's farm and $1,000 mortgage on improved orchard; several full-blood Nez Perces hold mortgages on white men's farms; younger generation educated in government schools where everything furnished free, never had to work or save; one young Nez Perce man ran through $17,000 leaving only $215.80 remaining; thrift class is rapidly squandering property in riotous living; about 300 of 300 fee patents issued last year resulted in sale or mortgage; mortgages seldom recorded; estimated 300 of 300 have sold or mortgaged; Nez Perces trust period of 25 years ended; 1400 Indians on reservation, only 50 earning all their own living; most live off lease rentals; leasing system is bad but no workable substitute; Fort Belknap Indians hold land in common but government was forced to feed them on horse meat; would not issue fee patents wholesale on any basis; Superintendents should designate those who should receive patents and submit list to Indian Office once or twice a year

testimony.witness_title: Superintendent, Fort Peck Indian Agency
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on fee patent policy
testimony.subject: Effect of fee patent policy; Fort Peck allotment history; Rocky Boy case study; criticism of bulk citizenship
testimony.key_claims: Vital mistakes made in handling Indian question; reservation system as developed may never have been allowed; Fort Peck Indians allotted only twelve years yet large number own absolutely nothing; only way to get real estate is to inherit it; they have shown inability to handle own property as class and as individuals; Rocky Boy Indians had 60 years of freedom and came to such poverty that people of state petitioned government to provide reservation; Rocky Boy Indians now most backward non-English speaking degraded tribe in state; result of sixty years of freedom; opposed to granting citizenship to Indians in the bulk; civil authorities very much dislike and often refuse to administer civil authority over Indians; each reservation and individual case should receive decision on own particular merit; in his mind best if every family maintains homestead to diminish floating population; since coming four years ago has allowed patents-in-fee to practically all young and mixed-blood Indians in accordance with what he supposed was the desire of the Office

testimony.witness_title: Field Clerk, Idabel, Oklahoma; Choctaw tribal member
testimony.hearing: Investigation Committee hearing
testimony.committee: Investigation Committee for the House Committee on Indian Affairs
testimony.date: unknown (some time last year prior to letter)
testimony.subject: Extension of period of restriction for Choctaw Indians; condition of Indians unable to handle their own affairs
testimony.key_claims: Snead appeared before the committee and was impressed that extension of the restriction period would be entertained only in cases of absolute necessity. He urged Congress to know the real condition and that failure to provide protection where needed would further the interests of those whose business it is to separate the Indian from his property. He was unalterably opposed to relinquishing supervision over those unable to handle their own affairs, particularly as the restriction period for Choctaw Indians was approaching termination in 1931.

testimony.witness_title: Superintendent, Fort Peck Indian Agency
testimony.hearing: unknown inquiry or survey
testimony.committee: Board of Indian Commissioners or Office of Indian Affairs
testimony.location: Fort Peck Indian Agency, Poplar, Montana
testimony.subject: Patent-in-fee policy, Indian competency, reservation conditions
testimony.key_claims: Superintendent described issuing patents-in-fee to practically all young and middle-aged people asking for them over four years, recommending only portions of allotments in most cases. Reported that in the great majority of cases Indians did nothing with the patents. Those made citizens by Competency Commission varied widely. Provided statistical data: 204 total patents issued (333 for full allotments, 196 for part allotments); 36 built homes; 31 purchased machinery and stock; 13 retained land; 56 had cash in bank; large numbers had nothing to show. Indians had lived on childrens moneys for four years and refused to work. Opposed bulk citizenship grants.

testimony.witness_title: Superintendent, Coeur d'Alene Indian Agency
testimony.hearing: unknown inquiry or survey
testimony.committee: Board of Indian Commissioners or Office of Indian Affairs
testimony.location: Coeur d'Alene Indian Agency, Sorrento, Idaho
testimony.subject: Patent-in-fee issuance policy at Coeur d'Alene Reservation
testimony.key_claims: Lawshe reported 139 patents-in-fee issued to original allottees; 55 classified as whites; 48 issued prior to 1916; of 91 issued since 1916, 54 lost their land; 22 doing fairly well but dependent on rental income from ward family members; 15 with no record; only 12 doing fairly well overall. One full-blood with little education purchased additional land and is farming family land. Many patents led to immediate sale, trade for automobile, or mortgage. Ordinary method upon receiving patent is to mortgage the land; proceeds consumed quickly. Recommended patent only after Indian demonstrates self-support through farming or other gainful occupation. Did not believe blood quantum or years of schooling should be the gauge for competency.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Holdenville, Oklahoma
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners survey
testimony.subject: Policy on releasing Indians from government supervision; Creek and Seminole Indians
testimony.key_claims: Youngblood described large-scale land fraud following the 1908 Act removing restrictions. Reported 1,600 mixed-blood allotments in Hughes County each appraised at $1,040; estimated 75% of mixed-blood Indians defrauded of 70% of allotment value; total losses estimated at $873,600 in Hughes County and $544,320 in Seminole County. Cited nine specific cases of fraud. Favored holding restrictions during allottee lifetime or until proven ability to provide for family. Advocated for repeal of laws facilitating land transfer without protection. Described land grafters as demanding Indians be turned loose. Witnessed historical transformation of tribes from tepees to modern homes.

testimony.witness_title: Field Clerk, Idabel, Oklahoma
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners survey response
testimony.subject: Competency of Choctaw Indians; individual vs. blanket removal of restrictions
testimony.key_claims: Snead reported first competency commission visited in 1917; some recipients already demonstrated business management capacity while others were intelligent but poor managers. Commission made two subsequent visits. Submitted approximately 35 names of adult half-blood Indians for restriction removal. Observed that restrictions removed from Indians doing well led to their undoing. Half-blood Indians not actually half-blood in lineage immediately disposed of property. Full-blood educated boys also immediately sold property. Estimated 90% of land sold or encumbered above earning capacity among those released from control. Concluded 50% either retained land, bought other land, or engaged in business. Greatest cause of failure is graft machinery; allotments valued $5,000-$10,000 entirely at disposal of unprepared individuals. Favored liberal policy for competent Indians and protection for others. In favor of unconditional removal for half-blood or less if properly enrolled and of average intelligence.

testimony.witness_title: Field Clerk, Sallisaw, Oklahoma
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on removal of restrictions
testimony.subject: Unconditional removal of restrictions from Cherokee Indians
testimony.key_claims: Has been in service at Sallisaw more than eight years. District has approximately 1,600 restricted Indians including minors. Restrictions unconditionally removed through regular channels in about 60 cases; by competency commissions 105 cases; by Departmental order covering half-blood Indians approximately 100 cases. Education of coming generation is most important. Full-blood Indian children at great disadvantage attending public schools. Recommends encouraging attendance at Government schools. Urges that removal of restrictions not be done as a class proposition.

testimony.witness_title: U.S. Field Clerk, Muskogee, Oklahoma
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on removal of restrictions
testimony.subject: Unconditional removal of restrictions from Creek, Cherokee and Choctaw Indians
testimony.key_claims: Has been employed in office of Superintendent for Five Civilised Tribes about ten years, Field Clerk in Muskogee/McIntosh/Haskell County district for more than four years. Since fall of 1918, about 200 Indians granted unconditional removal by competency commission and about 125 half-blood Indians by blanket order of Secretary of Interior. Approximately one-fifth of adult Indians under restrictions in 1918. Of 100 personally known Indians with restrictions removed, 65 sold land and dissipated proceeds, 35 retained land or purchased other land. Only about 10% would be classed as success. Competency commissions too lenient. Opposes blanket removal of restrictions. Notes that many competent Indians refuse removal of restrictions citing treaty obligations. Recommends competency commission work in conjunction with local field representative. Commission should visit Indians in their homes.

testimony.witness_title: Field Clerk, Stilwell, Oklahoma
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on removal of restrictions
testimony.subject: Unconditional removal of restrictions from Cherokee Indians
testimony.key_claims: About 400 families of Cherokee Indians in district. Opposes removal of restrictions as a class proposition. About 60% of Indians whose restrictions removed by competency commissions have disposed of or encumbered property so title is in jeopardy. Approximately 75% of Indians enrolled as 2 degree of blood released by Departmental order have sold or mortgaged allotments. Removal from this class a serious mistake. Removal as a class based on degree of blood is often incorrect. By Act of Congress all Cherokee citizens become unrestricted in 1931, which is entirely too soon. Full-blood Indians would rather die than ask for assistance from white people. Agitation to free all Indians originated from grafters and unscrupulous merchants and lawyers. Full-blood Indian has inherent weakness in moral fibre and is easiest person to influence. Recommends gradual freedom through Field Clerk and careful competency commission.

testimony.witness_title: Field Clerk, McAlester, Oklahoma
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on removal of restrictions
testimony.subject: Unconditional removal of restrictions from Choctaw Indians
testimony.key_claims: Recommends handling each individual case strictly on its merits. Unconditional removal of restrictions from Indian citizens would result in wreck and ruin of most of them. Some old ignorant full-bloods safer to turn loose than young educated full-bloods. Majority of people associate with Indians do not set good example. Many Indians own land in other counties where they do not live and receive little benefit; suggests that land should be sold or restrictions removed to allow use of funds in home community. Believes restrictions should be removed from surplus land not occupied, while living conditions improved and made sanitary.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Eufaula, Oklahoma
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on removal of restrictions
testimony.subject: Unconditional removal of restrictions from Creek, Cherokee and Choctaw Indians
testimony.key_claims: In Indian Service since 1913: three years Cantonment Agency with Cheyenne and Arapahoes, three years Kiowa Agency with Kiowas, Comanches and Apaches, past 13 months Union Agency at Muskogee. Work brought direct contact with Indians of various tribes. Restricted full-blood Indians live in Indian community, withdrawn from white citizenship, unable to speak or write English. Unconditional removal would invite hordes of land grafters to invade Indian country. When Indian can speak read and write English should be given full citizenship. In most cases Indians given full citizenship sold land and squandered money. Department has not removed restrictions from Indian not sufficiently intelligent to make his way. Unconditional removal from all classes would not cooperate with Department's present system.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Atoka, Oklahoma
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on removal of restrictions
testimony.subject: Unconditional removal of restrictions from Choctaw Indians
testimony.key_claims: Recommends not turning loose too much at once. After land and money is gone it is too late. Restrictions should be removed from small part of surplus land, 40 or 80 acres at a time, in most cases sold with money spent for Indians through Indian Office. Would be governed by value of land. In cases of old and feeble Indians with no money, should sell land piece at a time and give money as needed. Does not think any white man he has met would not like to see restrictions removed - they want Indians to pay taxes and work roads.

testimony.witness_title: Temporary Farmer, Ardmore, Oklahoma
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on removal of restrictions
testimony.subject: Unconditional removal of restrictions from Chickasaw Indians
testimony.key_claims: Fully 80% of Indians turned loose have wasted all that was given to them and have nothing to show. Indians do not live to work, are easily influenced, majority of associates do not set good example. Business men advise Indians to make bad investments when in white man's favor. Indians do not appreciate value of property until it is gone. Five Civilised Tribes would be much better off financially if there never had been any restrictions removed. In another way, having restrictions removed made better citizens of some who then became willing to do honest labor. Worst enemy of Indians in this section is whiskey and various other intoxicants.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Poteau, Oklahoma
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on removal of restrictions
testimony.subject: Unconditional removal of restrictions from Choctaw Indians
testimony.key_claims: Turning Indians loose without government supervision would be a sad mistake. There is always a grafter ready to buy at small figure, borrow, beg or steal whatever Indian has privilege to sell. Indians who did well after restriction removal are part white, inheriting ability to take care of themselves. Those doing well after removal often insist full-bloods get restrictions removed so they can exploit them. Would not be possible to change customs and manner of living of a race of people in short time. Until Indians become imbued with desire to better living conditions no wholesale removal of restrictions should be considered.

testimony.witness_title: Indian Service employee dealing with Hughes County
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on removal of restrictions
testimony.subject: Fraud against mixed-blood Creek Indians in Hughes County and Seminole County
testimony.key_claims: In Hughes County there were 1,600 mixed blood allotments of 160 acres, appraised value $1,040 each. Very small percent of mixed-blood Indians received anything like fair consideration for allotments. Nine specific cases documented. Estimated 75% of mixed-blood Indians of Hughes County defrauded out of 70% of value of allotments. 1,200 mixed-bloods in Hughes County lost estimated $873,600. 567 mixed-blood Seminoles lost estimated $544,320. These figures are extremely low and investigation would show larger amounts. Full-blood Seminoles disposed of land when turned loose. Competency commission turning Indians loose including those unable to speak English. Most important work is training in industrial lines and educating rising generation, not merely supervision of property.

testimony.witness_title: Temporary Farmer, Ardmore, Oklahoma
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on patent-in-fee and restriction policy
testimony.committee: Board of Indian Commissioners / Office of Indian Affairs
testimony.subject: Removing restrictions from Five Civilized Tribes Indians
testimony.key_claims: Would be governed by value of land in deciding whether to sell. Poor rough land worth only a couple dollars an acre not worth selling in small tracts. In some cases would remove restrictions and let Indian sell with understanding that if he makes good and invests properly, restrictions would be removed from other land later. Old and feeble Indians with no money to live on should be allowed to sell land a piece at a time. Believes 80 percent of Indians have wasted all property given them. Removal of all restrictions would mean great poverty. Has not met a white man who would not like to see restrictions removed - they are jealous of Indians and want them to pay taxes and work roads.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Poteau, Oklahoma
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on patent-in-fee and restriction policy
testimony.committee: Board of Indian Commissioners / Office of Indian Affairs
testimony.subject: Turning Indians loose without Government supervision
testimony.key_claims: Turning Indians loose without supervision would be a sad mistake. There is always some grafter ready to buy, borrow, beg or steal whatever the Indian has privilege to sell. It would be all right if all men were honest but people think it is not wrong to cheat the Indian. Five Civilized Tribes would be better off financially if there never had been any restrictions removed. Knows several cases where restrictions were removed and Indians have nothing to show for proceeds. However in another way believes it made better citizens out of some Indians - once they sold and became broke, some thought themselves too good to work but then found honest labor. Knows some who sold allotments who now depend entirely on labor for living. Indians of Five Civilized Tribes have full citizenship in regard to voting and holding office. As fast as restricted Indians prove themselves competent they should be turned loose. Worst enemy is whiskey, corn whiskey, Jake, and various intoxicants and dope.

testimony.witness_title: Agency Farmer, Colville Indian Reservation, Omak, Washington
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on patent-in-fee policy
testimony.committee: Board of Indian Commissioners / Office of Indian Affairs
testimony.subject: Success or failure of patent-in-fee policy at Colville
testimony.key_claims: Economic or financial competency is not a tangible possession like education or degree of blood. Majority of Indians and majority of white people do not have excessive acquisitiveness - most wealth is in hands of small percentage. Believes in liberal policy on patent-in-fee issuance. When an Indian desires a patent it argues financial incompetence or that economic disadvantage of paying taxes outweighs benefit of land ownership dignity. Six cases out of ten the actual reason for requesting patent is to get control of land to secure money by sale or mortgage. Policy of wholesale patent issuance serves as education to entire tribe about risk of losing allotments. Negative examples are more noticeable than positive steady-going Indians who retain land. Submitted reports of three district farmers.

testimony.witness_title: Agency Farmer, Colville Indian Reservation, Inchelium, Washington
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on patent-in-fee policy
testimony.committee: Board of Indian Commissioners / Office of Indian Affairs
testimony.subject: Benefits or disadvantages of fee patents in Inchelium district
testimony.key_claims: District has larger percentage of mixed-blood Indians. Degree of blood has very little influence on whether patent was beneficial. Full-bloods have made good after patent and some with very little Indian blood have dissipated allotments. Majority of cases where patents issued have been beneficial or at least not detrimental.
