All adult competent Indians in district have already received patents. Some competent Indians do not desire patents because of added tax burden. Best to examine each individual case on its merits, with field employee's judgment as basis. Names Theodore Bourgeau, Victor Dupuie, Barney Richard, Peter Noyes, Nancy Moore, D.L. Skeels as successful cases. Names Willie Ferguson, Marcelle Lafleur, Henry Stensgar, Joseph Noel as detrimental cases. Joseph Mullen a nuanced case - sold allotment but improved other land.

testimony.witness_title: Agency Farmer, Colville Indian Reservation, Nespelem, Washington
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on patent-in-fee policy
testimony.committee: Board of Indian Commissioners / Office of Indian Affairs
testimony.subject: Condition of patent-in-fee Indians in Nespelem district
testimony.key_claims: Of 17 Indians in Nespelem district, 11 have sold their allotments and only 3 have anything of value to show for the money. In some cases disposition was justified because lands were not agricultural and could not furnish a living. Describes Charley Bob farming father's and deceased mother's allotments, built house/barn/fence/alfalfa, in heavy debt, original allotment only grazing land worth about $1,000. Ross Hilleary sold allotment, borders McGinnis Lake, now used for irrigation with 80 tillable acres, bought a car. Tom Andrews traded part of allotment for Ford car, owes Government $644.88. Sam Friedlander sold allotment to brother's wife for $2500. William Friedlander still on allotment with 100 acres cultivation, sold 25 cattle and used proceeds to improve allotment. Paul Smitakin farming father's allotment, working as forest guard, plans business college. Charley Hilburn traded allotment for King Eight car, good mechanic but not energetic. Hiram Runnels sold north half of allotment, now on child's allotment, awaiting appointment to US Dry Squad. Arcasa boys sold grazing land allotments, well educated and employed. Bill Condon competent, holds and leases allotment, successful stock raiser. Dan Condon sold allotment for about $2,000, now in stock raising. Whitelaw brothers John, Pete and George successful in farming and stock raising, accumulated 100 head of cattle. Pakatas boys Mose and Philip each sold allotments for $10,000, money going fast.

testimony.witness_title: Agency Farmer, Fort Peck Agency, Poplar, Montana
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on patent-in-fee policy
testimony.committee: Board of Indian Commissioners / Office of Indian Affairs
testimony.subject: Patent-in-fee Indians at Fort Peck Reservation
testimony.key_claims: Patents-in-fee have been issued to Indians without enough thought about future conditions. Most patent-in-fee Indians he knows have failed. About 50 percent who received patents after board review are making good, retaining land, stock, implements and homes. Most patent-in-fee Indians sold land and first bought automobile, then some farm machinery and stock. When cash ran out they sold stock and machinery, last the automobile. Indians on reservation have been allotted only a short time and for several years after allotments no land was leased or income received. Not expected that in short time people would know how to handle land or money. Indians had no responsibility or business training. No patent should be given to entire allotment - homestead of 30 to 40 acres should be held in trust indefinitely. Patents should not be issued without application being passed on by competent board that has known applicant for at least several years. Superintendent fell in with Office desire to issue patents profusely as matter of loyalty. Some Indians objected to citizenship because they desired to keep property exempt from taxation. Others dissatisfied because they have lost their heritage. Bad practice of living off children's money should be prohibited except in very extreme cases. Names specific successful cases: William Manning, David Manning, Francis and Alfred Murray, Charles Seeds, Daniel Courchene, Fred Bauer, Traffle Sears. Names failed cases: Joe Alvarez, John Anderson, John Bruguior, William Boyd.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Box Elder Sub-agency, Brockton, Montana, Fort Peck Reservation
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on patent-in-fee policy
testimony.committee: Board of Indian Commissioners / Office of Indian Affairs
testimony.subject: Conditions of patent-in-fee Indians on Fort Peck Reservation
testimony.key_claims: Issuance of fee patents to Indians declared as citizens with expectation of making them self-supporting has been a failure to a large extent on this reservation. Conditions were far better for Indians before they were given citizenship because of Government control and protection from land selling. Almost without exception, Indians made citizens and given patent to all their land are selling allotments outright or mortgaging them for part cash and an automobile. Indians use automobiles for joy rides until all spent, then lose land. Pattern of coming back to superintendent to request patents on additional allotments after first is lost. Conditions for past several years in this vicinity have been bad for 90 percent of white people too. In future patents should not be issued so freely - more careful examination of character needed and homestead should be retained. Cites specific cases including John Bruguior addicted to drink, dissipated everything. Present practice of issuing patents is most too liberal.

testimony.witness_title: unknown field officer
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on restriction policy
testimony.committee: Board of Indian Commissioners / Office of Indian Affairs
testimony.subject: Advisability of removing all restrictions from Indians and letting them have their property
testimony.key_claims: In reply to letter of 5th inst. inquiring about removing all restrictions. 80 percent of Indians have wasted all that was given to them and have nothing to show. Indians do not live right, are easily influenced. People associating with them do not set good example, tell them Indian Service people just have easy jobs and are doing the skinning. Some people do all they can to influence Indians against Indian Service employees and their advice. Business men quite often advise Indians to make bad investments when it benefits white men. It would be all right if all men would tell the truth, but most people think it is not wrong to cheat the Indian.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Box Elder Sub-agency, Fort Peck Reservation
testimony.hearing: Survey of patent-in-fee conditions
testimony.subject: Overall failure of patent-in-fee policy on Fort Peck Reservation
testimony.key_claims: Issuance of fee patents has been a failure to a large extent on Fort Peck Reservation. Almost without exception Indians given patents sold their allotments or mortgaged them for cash and automobiles. Conditions were far better under Government control. Recommends retaining 40 acres in trust for each individual. Would personally inspect each Indian's capacity before issuing patent. Provides individual case reports on Manning, Murray, Seeds, Alvarez, Courchene, Bauer, Sears, Anderson, Bruguior, Boyd, and others.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Rosebud Indian Agency, Morrie/Morris, South Dakota
testimony.hearing: Survey of patent-in-fee conditions
testimony.subject: Conditions of 33 patent-in-fee Indians in Blackpipe District over 8.5 years
testimony.key_claims: Full-bloods not successful with patents. Quarter breeds sometimes retained land. Thomas Larvie and John Cordier squandered land. Fred Ashley, Harris Tell and others patented in 1913 spent money within 6 months and left reservation. Recommends each Indian retain minimum 100 acres; strenuous examination before future patents; very few Indians in district capable of managing own business.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Rosebud Indian Reservation, Little White River, South Dakota
testimony.hearing: Survey of patent-in-fee conditions
testimony.location: Little White River District, South Dakota
testimony.subject: All but four patent-in-fee Indians in district squandered land
testimony.key_claims: With exception of four, all patent-in-fee Indians in Little White River District squandered land and have nothing left except sometimes an old broken automobile. First thing most do is get drunk. Only four still have their land.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Rosebud Indian Agency, Wososo, South Dakota
testimony.hearing: Survey of patent-in-fee conditions
testimony.subject: Observations on Sioux patent-in-fee Indians; recommendation for policy on land retention
testimony.key_claims: Majority of Sioux know what to do but lack will power. They spend money as fast as possible. Should not be allowed to sell inherited lands as fast as white people will buy. Indians should hold original allotments for at least 35 more years. Some mortgage land for third or fourth class automobile, loan company gets land for a song. Some who received patents have settled into white community and are successful members.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Rosebud Indian Agency, Rosebud, South Dakota
testimony.hearing: Survey of patent-in-fee conditions
testimony.subject: No more than 10% of approximately 800 Rosebud patent-in-fee Indians successful; specific case reports
testimony.key_claims: Of approximately 800 patent-in-fee Indians on Rosebud, no more than 10% have managed affairs successfully. William Simpson and wife both patent-in-fees with no home, only two teams of horses and wagon. William Bordeaux and wife have no home, living hand to mouth. Todd Smith sold about $13,000 worth of land over ten years, has only a $300 house and works for Indian trader. Recommends 40 acres retained in trust, clause compelling Indian to build house, individual examination for competency.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Rosebud Indian Agency, Hamill, South Dakota
testimony.hearing: Survey of patent-in-fee conditions
testimony.subject: Indians will make no progress until placed on own resources; case examples near Hamill
testimony.key_claims: Indian will make no material progress until placed fully on own resources. Has no definite value for things since he never had to work. What incentive to work when children already have 160 acres allotted? Many Indians who squandered patents eventually settled into white community as members. Nearly all more than half-white have succeeded. 59 names submitted of Indians benefited by patents near Hamill, Colome, Winner, Dallas, and Dison.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Rosebud Indian Agency, Okreek, South Dakota (formerly Standing Rock)
testimony.hearing: Survey of patent-in-fee conditions
testimony.subject: Almost all Standing Rock patent-in-fee Indians failed; Nation Flying as sole success; young worker as example of recovery
testimony.key_claims: All Standing Rock patent-in-fee Indians spent all they had, sold land and stock, made trouble, would not work, implicated in crimes and cattle rustling, worse off than under trust. Only Nation Flying made good - bought farming tools, tractor, farmed 160 acres, refused $9,000 for half section. Full-blood office worker received patent, sold it, bought car, spent funds, came back to work and is now best worker. Success not solely due to white blood.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Ponca District, Rosebud Reservation, Herrick, South Dakota
testimony.hearing: Survey of patent-in-fee conditions
testimony.subject: Trust patent Indians far better off than patent-in-fee Indians on Standing Rock; individual competency examination needed
testimony.key_claims: Trust patent Indians on Standing Rock far better off than those with fee patents. All trust patent Indians have farms, cattle, horses, some farming 160 acres with milk cows, chickens, pigs. Very few Indians in district who received patents did not sell and blow money quickly. Small number retained land and making homes. Real estate men pester Indians until they sell. Should not turn all loose; judiciously issued patents with restrictions could work.

testimony.witness_title: unknown, Fort Peck Agency, Poplar, Montana
testimony.hearing: Survey of patent-in-fee conditions
testimony.subject: Standing Rock Reservation patent-in-fee history; approximately 600 patents issued; mixed results
testimony.key_claims: Approximately 600 patents issued on Standing Rock beginning before 1915, largely to mixed blood element who were educated and competent. Practically all of this land was disposed of. 1916 issuances dealt with those successful in industrial work but most of that land also disposed of. Land being something new, Indians permitted themselves to be involved in mortgages that ate up resources. Only one earlier patentee able to regain allotment. Many Indians who received patents later acquired lands in own name but these were subsequently mortgaged. Children of 1908-1909 allottees grew up with little knowledge of allotments often miles from home. Location of allotments made them of no possible use to recipients.

testimony.witness_title: Superintendent and S.D.A., Standing Rock Reservation
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on fee patent policy
testimony.subject: Effects of fee patent issuance at Standing Rock Reservation
testimony.key_claims: Approximately 600 fee patents issued at Standing Rock prior to and including 1916. Early patents were mortgaged and lands subsequently lost. Mixed blood allottees issued patents in 1916 were well-educated but nearly all disposed of land. Mortgages with accumulating interest consumed resources. Allotments made under Enabling Act of 1905 to heads of families along waterways became home sites; children allotted land miles away with no use for it. Land for older Indians worth $20-30/acre; children's land worth not exceeding $10/acre. White land speculators used unethical practices to induce sales. Believes degree of blood not a measure of competency; cases should be judged individually. Believes fee patents beneficial for Indian independence and self-reliance despite land losses. Only one Indian known who was able to regain his allotment. Ninety percent of unmarried/children allottees received land miles from homes. Recommends continuing fee patent issuance to competent Indians. Leasing home allotments should not be permitted.
testimony.questioner: Board of Indian Commissioners (via circular letter March 31, 1921)

testimony.witness_title: Superintendent, Yakima Indian Agency, Fort Simcoe, Washington
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on fee patent policy
testimony.location: Yakima Indian Agency, Fort Simcoe, Washington
testimony.subject: Patent-in-fee statistics and farmer reports, Yakima Reservation 1917-1920
testimony.key_claims: Submitted table of patent cases 1917-1920 showing sold, retained, and mortgaged. Large percentage of patents covered original allotments; land largely average agricultural or irrigable. Some parties disposed of land immediately upon patent; others mortgaged multiple times until full value extracted then deeded. Transmitting reports from three designated farmers. Spendthrift type Indians bought automobiles regardless of intelligence or industrial capacity; funds depleted and automobiles sold; these Indians invariably sell land for cash. Their general condition is no worse than before restrictions removed; experience has sobered most and placed them on own resources. Recommends issuing fee patents to all adult able-bodied mixed-blood allottees. Full-blood class of middle age, sober and industrious should be encouraged. Young full-blood educated men and women (24-25 years old) who read and write should be issued patents early before family influence retards them.
testimony.questioner: Board of Indian Commissioners (via circular letter March 31, 1921)

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Yakima Indian Reservation, White Swan, Washington
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on fee patent policy
testimony.subject: Personal observations after nine years service on patent-in-fee Indians at Yakima
testimony.key_claims: As a general rule Indians who received patents have progressed more rapidly than under Government jurisdiction because they recognize responsibility of managing own affairs. More independent; rely less on Government. Children entering public schools associating with white children. Indians have been too much pampered. Government owes protection to some dependent people but should treat them as wards. Indians now farming lands themselves instead of having lands leased to whites. Recommends issuing patents to all adult able-bodied mixed-blood allottees. Believes present system of leasing restricted inherited lands is burdensome and not logical. Field officers should negotiate leases and collect rents without so many procedural steps. Recommends issuing fee patents for portion of original allotments retaining reasonable acreage for home purposes in trust.
testimony.questioner: Board of Indian Commissioners (via circular letter)

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Yakima Reservation, Toppenish, Washington
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on fee patent policy
testimony.subject: Effects of fee patents at Yakima Reservation; automobile purchases and land disposal
testimony.key_claims: Most patent-in-fee Indians used poor judgment; either sold or mortgaged land and made poor use of money. As soon as Indian gets money, car salesmen approach him. Indian exchanges old car for new car and pays difference in cash. Department used good judgment in granting patents to competent Indians but thinks most are worse off today than under Government control. For good of the country would turn Indians loose but for this particular reservation's Indians land should be reserved for a period of years. Submitted five names of Indians who received patents. Cannot blame Indians entirely as they are subject to predatory white influence.
testimony.questioner: Board of Indian Commissioners (via circular letter)

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Yakima Reservation, Wapato, Washington
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on fee patent policy
testimony.subject: Condition of patent-in-fee Indians at Yakima Reservation
testimony.key_claims: No suffering has resulted as most are young and able to work or have inherited interests providing revenue. Even if reduced to working it would be best for them in long run. Some have sold or mortgaged land and spent money foolishly and are in dire financial straits. This has had effect on others who have been benefited by mistakes of others and are holding lands and saving money. Most resident Indians whose restrictions removed are farming lands directly or indirectly. High rents of past few years were no incentive for Indian to work but farming conditions have slumped and rentals decreasing proportionately. Does not think they are going too fast in releasing Indians from Government protection. Recommends: (1) individual competency examination; (2) hold back at least 20 acres as permanent homestead in trust; (3) sell all inherited land; (4) do not issue patents to old people but hold allotments in trust unless necessary for support; (5) Indians are more satisfied since becoming citizens. Indians who have received patents have slipped back in old groove with little regret or have improved condition.
testimony.questioner: Board of Indian Commissioners (via circular letter)

testimony.witness_title: Superintendent, Flathead Indian Reservation, Dixon, Montana
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on fee patent policy
testimony.subject: Statistical and qualitative report on 1004 patent-in-fee Indians at Flathead Reservation
testimony.key_claims: 1004 Indians received patents to original allotments; 31 allotments patented to heirs; allotments 80-160 acres each agricultural or grazing. Year-by-year issuance from 1910-1921. Assumed charge March 1921; found not much information on patent-in-fee Indian status. After inquiry: approximately 75% disposed of original allotments. Those retaining lands are progressive successful farmers comparing favorably with average white citizens; some (~35%) who disposed of lands purchased other property including farm lands. About 25% settled down making comfortable livings on leased lands or for wages. Balance loafing off rentals of children's lands or waiting for tribal payments. Citizenship cannot safely be granted en masse. Degree of blood no criterion; graduation from non-reservation school insufficient qualification. Most pronounced failures were young educated fellows and returned soldiers. Conditions vary greatly on different reservations and in different districts. Attitude of whites toward Indians important factor. In some localities predatory whites consider Indians only as legitimate prey using questionable methods to acquire property. An Indian safe to issue patent in one locality would certainly fail in another. Only safe course is individual case examination with superintendent's judgment followed.
testimony.questioner: Board of Indian Commissioners (via circular letter March 31, 1921)

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Ronan, Montana, Flathead Reservation
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on fee patent policy
testimony.subject: Status of 78 patent-in-fee Indians in St. Ignatius District, Flathead Reservation
testimony.key_claims: Report on 78 out of 33 (possibly 78 total reviewed) patent-in-fee Indians in St. Ignatius District: 45 (58%) sold land and spent money; 22 (28%) retained land and doing well; 7 sold land and invested proceeds; 4 mortgaged property. Those doing without exception just as they did before patents: successful farmers still successful, those living off rents still doing so, those who dissipated proceeds working for passable living. Some always looking forward to tribal payments making no effort while money coming. Cannot recall any Indians in territory who really bettered themselves since cut from Government control. Would suggest for adults turning them loose for country's benefit but reserving land for period of years for Indians. Where allottee could read and write, was intelligent, and not confirmed drunkard, would give patent. Each case dealt with separately on merits. Percentage of success same among Indians as whites but more attention paid when Indian dissipates allotment than when white man fails. Served as member of competency commissions for two years; convinced judgment of average superintendent in charge for few years should be followed.
testimony.questioner: Board of Indian Commissioners (via circular letter)

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Flathead Indian Reservation, Polson, Montana
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on fee patent policy
testimony.subject: Specific cases of patent-in-fee Indians at Flathead Reservation, Polson area
testimony.key_claims: Many Indians sold allotments for less than appraised value; nearly all money spent leaving Indians without income. Frank McLeod and Alex McLeod had land under private water rights and timothy; secured patents, moved to town, invested in automobiles, soon penniless. Four families depending entirely on tribal payments: Frank McLeod, Alex McLeod, Louis Clairmont Jr., Gilbert Burland - all had good allotments but did not make a living on them. After disposing of own allotments and wives' allotments, they work common labor until tribal payment in sight then cease working. Successful cases in same town: Mary Duplessis (lady's furnishing store), Duncan Campbell (feed barn and pool hall), Sam Pierre (farming and stock raising), Harry Burland (garage man), Mose Delaware (farming and clerking), Edna Hull (nurse in hospital). Joseph R. sold allotment for $3000, spent money, now living off mother's bounty and wife's allotment rent. Joseph Antiste sold allotment, broke in less than one month, now destitute, does not drink but may gamble, does not know how to work. Joseph Gardipie sold allotment, spent money, now broke. Louison Ashley sold allotment, bought saw mill, failed, bought separator and engine, failed at threshing, now broke. Fred Paricole exception: sold allotment, got laundry work from reform school training, employed over a year, married, doing well. Victor Dupuis farming allotment with threshing machine, well improved. Caville Dupuis farming allotment, owns threshing machine, doing well. Above-mentioned Indians of both classes are full-bloods; many others in both classes are mixed-bloods who appear presentable but cannot handle own affairs. Majority of Indians cannot be satisfied no matter what is done; dissatisfaction caused by agitators.
testimony.questioner: Board of Indian Commissioners (via circular letter)

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Flathead Reservation, Arlee, Montana
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners Inquiry on Patent-in-Fee Indians
testimony.subject: Condition of patent-in-fee Indians on Flathead Reservation; policy recommendations for releasing Indians from Government control
testimony.key_claims: Would issue patents-in-fee to all Indians of one-half or less Indian blood who had attained majority. Would not reserve any part of allotments for home sites since no Indian in district could make a living on ten or twenty acres. Four families (Frank McLeod, Alex McLeod, Louis Clairmont Jr., Gilbert Burland) depending almost entirely on tribal payments. Multiple allottees sold land and became destitute. Others (Mary Duplessis, Duncan Campbell, Sam Pierre, Harry Burland, Mose Delaware, Edna Hull) making comfortable living without selling allotments. About 49 patent-in-fee Indians in Polson district. Provided breakdown of patents delivered by year from 1908 to 1930. Most patentees retaining allotments are doing fairly well; some doing better than white people. Full-bloods do not stay in one place long enough to require home sites.

testimony.witness_title: Superintendent, Sisseton Agency, Sisseton, South Dakota
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners Inquiry on Patent-in-Fee Indians
testimony.subject: Conditions of patent-in-fee Indians at Sisseton; policy on releasing Indians from Government control
testimony.key_claims: Nearly all who received patents lost their land - only a negligible number retained it. Main reason Indians apply for patents is to sell the land. In most cases Indians receive adequate price but spend proceeds on subsistence, clothing, automobiles. About half the reservation is full-bloods. All mixed-bloods of one-half or less blood received patents for allotments. After selling land, many Indians leave reservation and find employment. Some Indians are 'parasites' who will not work regardless of opportunity. Policy is to disregard blood or educational status and require Indians to show by their own efforts they should not be held under Bureau control. Speeding up process of turning Indians loose regardless of competency should be materially curbed.

testimony.witness_title: Superintendent, Potawatomi Agency, Mayetta, Kansas
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners Inquiry on Patent-in-Fee Indians
testimony.subject: Patent-in-fee policy; conditions of Potawatomi patentees; competency standards
testimony.key_claims: 15 years of service in Bureau of Indian Affairs confirms that speeding up process of turning Indians loose regardless of competency should be materially curbed. Potawatomi tribe has about 730 enrolled, 813 allotments made on three rolls (first 39 years ago, last 16 years ago). In 1918, 43 allottees given patents by competency board. Total of approximately 177 patents issued. About one-third deceased; of remaining two-thirds all but 10-12 have sold land. 85% of patentees either sold land or have it mortgaged to approximately its value. Perhaps 50% of money received used paying old debts, remainder on automobiles, teams, wagons, harness, some small homes. About 25 patent-in-fee Indians holding and farming original allotments. Favors issuing patents to competent Indians regardless of blood status or education. Opposed to competency boards. An Indian who is able-bodied and able to work without wife and too many children dependent is competent. Many who squandered 10-12 thousand dollars each in last three years on fast living, arrested for intoxication, some in jails and penitentiaries.

testimony.witness_title: Superintendent, Fort Hall Reservation, Fort Hall, Idaho
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners Inquiry on Patent-in-Fee Indians
testimony.subject: Certificate of competency policy; conditions of Fort Hall Indians who received certificates
testimony.key_claims: Approximately 80% of Indians who received certificates of competency sold their land. Remaining 20% with very rare exceptions have mortgages on their land, some going through foreclosure, perhaps all will be within the next year. Does not know of any failure to make good in his district with one exception (Pete Lamoose). White people have been encouraging Indians to ask for certificates and have advanced money on strength of having lands turned over to them. Certificates often recommended to help Indians sell heirship land. Some instances where Indians sold land for about only one-third of market price. Would only issue certificates to Indians living on or near reservation; for those away only if permanently established elsewhere. Better class of Indians do not want certificates; see no necessity unless they wish to dispose of their holdings. Many Indians in Pocatello destitute after selling land. Each case should receive careful consideration before certificate granted on heirship land.

testimony.witness_title: Superintendent, Seger Indian Agency, Colony, Oklahoma
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners Inquiry on Patent-in-Fee Indians
testimony.subject: Results of Spring 1917 competency commission; conditions of patent-in-fee Indians at Seger Agency
testimony.key_claims: Spring 1917 competency commission visited and examined large number of Indians; result was exceedingly disastrous for each and every Indian who received patent. All allotments disposed of, some at ridiculously low prices. Indians disposed of land immediately upon receipt of patent (contracts to sell likely existing prior to patent receipt). Most allotments disposed of as soon as or very soon after receipt. Most Indians are penniless without exception and depend wholly on relatives or inherited interests for livelihood. Believes restricted Indians leasing land is better business proposition than working it themselves but believes farming own land is better than leasing even if less money. Too much money without effort is trouble with Indian race. Able-bodied Indians are better off when they have to work.

testimony.witness_title: Superintendent, Cantonment Indian Agency, Canton, Oklahoma
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners Inquiry on Patent-in-Fee Indians
testimony.subject: Patent-in-fee policy; conditions at Cantonment Agency
testimony.key_claims: Has been in charge since June 10, 1920 and recommended only one patent be issued direct. Department concurred and allottee was given patent to remaining 80 acres; she immediately sold for $6,000 (approximately market value) and used proceeds to purchase home in Anadarko; also voluntarily deposited $1500 with office. Many patents under this agency sold in accordance with Departmental regulations with proceeds expended under supervision. This plan is much preferable and more advantageous to Indian than issuing fee patents direct. Opposed to issuing patents in wholesale manner; each case should be considered on its merits regardless of quantum of Indian blood. Heirship estate allotments being sold under departmental regulations. Average Indian here will out-trade and beat average white man in business transactions.

testimony.witness_title: Superintendent, Seger Indian Agency
testimony.hearing: unknown investigation or survey
testimony.subject: Conditions of fee patent Indians at Seger Agency; land disposition outcomes; leasing vs. farming debate
testimony.key_claims: About 25 fee patent Indians holding original allotments and farming them at Seger Agency as of Spring 1917. Out of a total of approximately 220+ allotments, most land has been disposed of, some at ridiculously low prices. Indians disposed of land immediately upon receipt of patent, with contracts to sell likely existing prior to patent issuance. Believes restricted Indians better off leasing land than working it, but that farming own land is better than leasing. Attributes problems to Indians getting loans and mortgages on crops up to full value before harvest.

testimony.witness_title: Superintendent, Cantonment Indian Agency
testimony.hearing: unknown investigation or survey
testimony.subject: Fee patent issuance and outcomes; competency standards; opposition to wholesale patents; specific case of female allottee
testimony.key_claims: Has been in charge of jurisdiction since June 10, 1920, and recommended only one patent be issued direct in that time. Female allottee sold 80 acres for $6,000 (approximately actual value) and purchased home in Anadarko; deposited $1,500 with office. Opposed to issuing patents wholesale; each case should be considered on merits regardless of blood quantum. Fee patent Indians who disposed of allotments are without exception penniless and dependent on relatives or inherited interests. Competency commission examination results were exceedingly disastrous. Believes practice of issuing fee patents is pernicious. Opposed to turning over property to Indians of one-half or less blood without supervision. Believes Indians of any blood quantum who cannot conduct ordinary business should have restrictions maintained. States younger educated Indians, nine times out of ten, are interested only in having a good time. Older non-English speaking Indians need protection even in dealings with own children.

testimony.witness_title: Lease Clerk, Cantonment Indian Agency
testimony.hearing: unknown investigation or survey
testimony.subject: Living and working conditions of Cheyenne and Arapaho Indians; leasing practices; patent-in-fee outcomes; Indian education and incentives
testimony.key_claims: Has lived and worked among Cheyenne and Arapaho Indians for seven years (three as agency farmer, four as lease clerk). Majority of Indians have their lands leased as only income besides interests. Only a very few live on or cultivate portions of allotments; prefer to live in camps or villages. Lands cultivated are sown to forage crops requiring little labor. Very hard to get Indians to work when they have money to their credit. Condition attributed largely to custom of leasing lands instead of being taught or compelled to farm allotments. Not a single patent-in-fee Indian has retained possession of lands any length of time; most sold as soon as possible. Patent proceeds used to improve other inherited land interests. Believes if Indians reaching majority were given their inheritance unencumbered and made responsible for their own success, they would succeed. States returning school Indians lose ambition within months due to lack of incentives under government system. Indian receives better education and training than average white child; if given proper economic training is as competent as white brother. Blood quantum is not a fair test of competency; education is the only fair and equitable test. Without radical steps, Indians will become more helpless and beyond redemption. All able-bodied Indians better off when required to work.

mortgages.land_description: Standing Rock Reservation allotments, North Dakota
mortgages.context: Kitch reported mixed-blood Indians involved in mortgages whose interest and principal gradually ate up resources, necessitating disposal of land entirely

mortgages.borrower: Fee patent Indians on Crow Reservation (some who mortgaged land)
mortgages.context: Pearce reported nearly all fee patent holders who did not sell their land had mortgaged their land and speculated unwisely

mortgages.borrower: Fee patent Indians in Five Civilized Tribes
mortgages.land_description: Various allotments, Five Civilized Tribes, Oklahoma
mortgages.context: B. F. McCurtain estimated approximately 60% of Indians released from supervision by competency commission had either sold property or mortgaged it for all it is worth

mortgages.borrower: approximately 15% of Pine Ridge fee patent Indians
mortgages.amount: half to two-thirds of land value
mortgages.land_description: fee patented allotments at Pine Ridge Indian Reservation
mortgages.context: H.M. Tidwell reported approximately 15% more of Pine Ridge fee patent Indians have some equity in their lands having placed mortgages ranging from half to two-thirds of value of lands on them. Such cases practically always result in foreclosure.

Earlier patentees at Standing Rock involved themselves in mortgages; interest and principal gradually ate up their resources and it was necessary to dispose of land entirely. Mortgages and interest described as key mechanism of land loss.

mortgages.borrower: approximately 90% of Shoshone Reservation fee patent Indians
mortgages.land_description: allotments at Shoshone Indian Reservation, 80 acres average irrigable agricultural land
mortgages.context: E.H. Hutchison reported about 90% of 303 fee patent Indians at Shoshone Reservation have either sold or mortgaged their lands. Some few made beneficial use of proceeds.

mortgages.borrower: unnamed Indian described by J.W.C. Miller
mortgages.land_description: fee patented allotment, Pine Ridge area
mortgages.context: J.W.C. Miller described that if Indian cannot sell his land he will mortgage it and that is the end of it - cash used for supporting himself or traveling, does not improve home or purchase stock.

mortgages.land_description: Allotments at Shoshone Indian Reservation, Fort Washakie, Wyoming
mortgages.context: Approximately 90% of the 303 Shoshone fee patent recipients either sold or mortgaged their lands; those who mortgaged typically lost land when mortgage became due

mortgages.land_description: Allotments at Rosebud Indian Agency, South Dakota
mortgages.context: About 90% of Rosebud fee patent Indians immediately sold allotments or mortgaged them and sold when mortgage became due; allotment values ranged from $1000 to $16,000 with average of $4000 per quarter section

mortgages.land_description: Turtle Mountain allotments in western North Dakota and eastern Montana
mortgages.context: If mortgage placed on land, Indian made no sincere effort to repay loan; generally not even interest and taxes paid; Indian mortgages land then becomes discouraged, defaults in making payments, and finally loses land

Many younger class mortgage their lands; mortgages seldom recorded so no definite information; estimated 300 of 300 fee patents issued last year resulted in sale or mortgage; mortgage came due and land sold
Full-blood Nez Perce woman who cannot read write or speak English holds $13,000 first farm mortgage on white man's farm
Full-blood Nez Perce woman holds $1,000 mortgage on improved orchard tract owned by another white man

mortgages.land_description: non-reservation allotments in Montana and western North Dakota
mortgages.context: Indians mortgaged property and in more detrimental cases mortgaged the property; once an Indian mortgages chances are he will become discouraged, will default in making payments in full, and will finally lose the land; mortgage became due if not sooner land was sold
Indians either sold land or mortgaged it; mortgage became due and land was sold; nine out of ten sold land and spent proceeds

mortgages.land_description: 190-acre allotments, Inland Empire prairie and timber land, Coeur d'Alene Reservation
mortgages.context: Upon receiving patent, ordinary practice was to mortgage the land; many of the 56 reported as still having land had it badly mortgaged; of 91 patents issued since 1916 at Coeur d'Alene, twenty known to have been sold or lost through mortgages

mortgages.land_description: allotted lands at Fort Peck Reservation, Poplar, Montana
mortgages.context: Superintendent described ordinary pattern: upon receiving patent, Indians either sell land, trade it for an automobile, or mortgage it

mortgages.land_description: allotted lands in Idabel district valued $5,000-$10,000
mortgages.context: Snead reported 90% of land sold or encumbered for funds above earning capacity; allottees later obliged to sell

mortgages.borrower: Coeur d'Alene allottees receiving timber patents
mortgages.land_description: timber allotments at Coeur d'Alene Reservation
mortgages.context: Upon receiving patent after timber sale bringing thousands of dollars, practice is to mortgage the lands; no good times or money would be left as funds used for immediate needs

mortgages.borrower: Abijah Colbert and Richard Floyd Colbert
mortgages.land_description: garage property purchased after disposal of allotments
mortgages.context: The Colbert brothers, Chickasaw Roll Nos. 961 and 960, disposed of allotments, purchased a garage and assumed a $20,000 mortgage. When mortgage came due they would in all probability lose the garage. They graduated from Murry Agricultural School and attended Oklahoma A&M but lacked ability to handle own affairs.

mortgages.borrower: approximately 75% of half-blood Indians released by Departmental order
mortgages.context: About 75% of Indians enrolled as 2 degree of blood released from supervision by Departmental order have sold or mortgaged their allotments, putting title in jeopardy.

mortgages.borrower: Indians whose restrictions removed by competency commissions
mortgages.context: About 60% of Indians whose restrictions removed by competency commissions have either disposed of property or encumbered it such that title is in jeopardy. Property on which it is possible to obtain funds in times of stress is a temptation to Indians as well as white men.

mortgages.land_description: Willie Ferguson's allotment and wife's allotment, Colville Indian Reservation, Inchelium district
mortgages.context: Willie Ferguson mortgaged his allotment and also that of his wife; making no effort to farm; spent proceeds on automobiles

mortgages.land_description: Henry Stensgar's allotment, Colville Indian Reservation, Inchelium district
mortgages.context: Henry Stensgar received patent-in-fee and mortgaged his land; making no effort to redeem this land

mortgages.land_description: allotted lands, Colville Indian Reservation, Nespelem district
mortgages.context: Hughes reports Indians after securing fee patent mortgaged their land for additional farming equipment and put in larger crops; due to drought many have lost their places and are hopelessly in debt
Alvin Warrior reports almost without exception Indians given patents to all land are mortgaging them for part cash and an automobile

mortgages.borrower: unnamed Colville Indians generally - approximately 90 in Robinson district
mortgages.context: Robinson states many have lost their places and are hopelessly in debt; others still hanging on hoping to save land with good crop

mortgages.land_description: patented allotments on Fort Peck Reservation
mortgages.context: Patent-in-fee Indians mortgaging allotments for part cash and an automobile; lender eventually gets land at considerably less than actual value when Indian cannot meet obligation

F. E. Rogers describes Indians mortgaging land to get cash for automobiles; loan company gets land at considerably less than actual value when Indian cannot meet obligation; mortgage company gets land for a song

mortgages.land_description: patented allotments and subsequently acquired lands on Standing Rock Reservation
mortgages.context: Standing Rock patentees permitted themselves to be involved in mortgages, the interest and principal of which gradually ate up their resources; land was something new to them; subsequently acquired lands also mortgaged

mortgages.borrower: various patent-in-fee Indians (W. L. Gardner district)
mortgages.context: W. L. Gardner reports Indians mortgaging land for old third or fourth class automobiles; mortgage company gets the land for a song when Indian cannot pay

mortgages.amount: various; increased multiple times until full value extracted
mortgages.context: Many Standing Rock allottees mortgaged lands after receiving fee patents; mortgages were new to them and they permitted themselves to be involved; interest and principal gradually consumed resources; lands ultimately lost

mortgages.amount: various sums; sometimes increased several times until Indians received practically full value, whereupon deeds were given
mortgages.context: Don M. Carr's report: some parties first placed mortgages on land for various sums; mortgages increased multiple times until Indians received practically full value then deeds were given; effectively a mechanism of land transfer

mortgages.borrower: Flathead allottees (4 cases in St. Ignatius District)
mortgages.land_description: Allotments in St. Ignatius District, Flathead Reservation
mortgages.context: B. Brown's report: 4 out of 78 patent-in-fee Indians in St. Ignatius District recorded as having mortgaged their property

mortgages.borrower: approximately 20% of Fort Hall certificate-of-competency Indians
mortgages.land_description: individual allotments, Fort Hall Reservation, Idaho
mortgages.context: Donner reported remaining 20% who did not sell have mortgages on their land, some going through foreclosure proceedings, perhaps all will be within the next year

mortgages.amount: up to approximately full value of land
mortgages.context: A. R. Snyder reported 85% of patentees either sold land or have it plastered with mortgage up to about its value
Cited as one exception by Fort Hall superintendent as allottee who sold or mortgaged his allotment
White people encouraging Indians to ask for certificates of competency and advancing money on strength of having lands turned over to them on arrival of certificate
Perkins noted restricted Indians who farm their land begin to get loans and have mortgages on crops to their full value when ready to harvest

mortgages.land_description: allotments under Seger Indian Agency jurisdiction
mortgages.context: Superintendent Perkins states that restricted Indians who farm their own land begin to get loans and have mortgages on crops to their full value when crops are ready to harvest; cited as reason leasing may be preferable despite lower returns
